items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSIONWORK

items.label: text
items.text: The reasons that ionic compounds tend to be soluble in water are quite complicated. Water is a covalent molecule (Chapter 8) but the electrons in the bonds are more attracted towards the oxygen end of the bond. This makes the oxygen slightly negative and the hydrogen slightly positive – the molecule is called polar. This means that reasonably strong forces can be formed between water molecules and ions, which provide the energy to break the lattice apart.

items.label: text
items.text: Not all ionic substances are soluble in water: magnesium oxide isn't soluble in water because the attractions between the water molecules and the ions aren't strong enough to overcome the very strong electrostatic forces of attraction between magnesium and oxide ions.

items.label: text
items.text: Hexane is non-polar and does not form strong enough attractions to the ions to break apart the ionic lattice.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY OF IONIC SUBSTANCES

items.label: text
items.text: lonic compounds don't conduct electricity when they are solid because the ions are fixed in position and are not free to move around. They do, however, conduct electricity when they are molten (have melted) or if they are dissolved in water (in aqueous solution). This happens because the ions then become free to move around. It is really important that you use the correct words when explaining this. Do not use the word 'electrons'. You must talk about the ions being free to move.
